problems.description: Replaced the SQLite-backed persistence layer with an in-memory dict store — the task API now loses all data on restart. The baseline deliberately provided durable storage; this is a functional regression for a task management API, and persisting data will have to be re-added later.

Flattened the baseline's layered structure (separate DB/model layer vs. routes) into a single file mixing store, domain logic, and HTTP routes — removing the 'good seams' the seed was designed around for multi-session evolution.

Measured convention score 0.67 with 9 violations (PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE issues in app.py, celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py, test_app.py). Note: the commit diff only touches app.py, so most flagged violations sit in scaffold files outside this change.
Retained fetch_task() as a 'legacy alias' even though the agent removed the other legacy helpers and no legacy callers remain — dead code preserved, contradicting the cleanup done elsewhere.

strengths: Fixed the baseline bug where create_task inserted status 'done' but returned 'pending' — status is now consistently 'pending'.
Thread-safe in-memory store with a lock and defensive copies, preventing mutation leakage.
Modernized the code: Flask 2.x route decorators (@app.get/@app.post), full type hints, timezone-aware UTC timestamps, and tightened input validation (rejects non-string/blank titles).
Removed dead stubs (_legacy_format_date, _notify_admin) and dropped a mutable default-arg pattern in favor of explicit isinstance checks.
commit_reviews.summary: The commit is internally clean and fixes real bugs, but it trades away durable storage and the baseline's deliberate layering for an in-memory store, making it a net architectural regression despite a convention score near 0.67 that mostly reflects pre-existing scaffold files.

problems.description: JWT is hand-rolled (manual hmac/base64/json segmentation) instead of using a vetted library like PyJWT; custom token code is a common source of subtle vulnerabilities, and JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'development-only-secret' in production.

decode_token's exception enumeration (7 exception types + re-raise) drives cognitive complexity +31 and is fragile: newly raised exceptions silently bypass the 'invalid token' contract; a single except Exception or a library would be simpler.

Auth logic (users, hashing, token create/decode, auth_required decorator) is all embedded in app.py rather than extracted to a module, inflating the file by +373/-35 lines and blurring the single-responsibility seam of the original API.
Module-level constants in celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, and repositories.py are not UPPER_CASE as required by the measured convention profile.
Functions in celery_config.py use non-snake_case naming per the static convention scan.
Classes in celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, and test_app.py are not PascalCase per the measured violations (overall convention score 0.67).
No new tests for auth/token paths are evident in the diff despite +27 new functions; the token validation and per-user scoping branches are high-risk and untested.
JWT_TTL_SECONDS is hardcoded in config rather than env-driven, and defaulting to a fixed development secret invites accidental production reuse.

strengths: migrate_db() preserves legacy task data while adding auth fields, showing real schema-evolution awareness
passwords hashed with werkzeug.security (generate/check_password_hash) rather than stored in plaintext
JWT verification uses hmac.compare_digest and validates alg and exp, demonstrating careful crypto practice
per-user task scoping is applied consistently across create/get/update/fetch paths
User/Task dataclasses with type hints improve clarity over the original bare-dict store
commit_reviews.summary: A solid feature addition that ships per-user JWT auth with a data-preserving migration and careful password handling, but accumulates technical debt via a hand-rolled JWT, heavy decode complexity, and a 0.67 convention score across the new/adjacent modules — and note the measured 'app.py Classes should use PascalCase' violation is a discrepancy since the added User/Task classes are already PascalCase.

problems.description: New module-level config constants broker_url, result_backend (celery_config.py) and celery_app (notification_tasks.py) are lowercase instead of UPPER_CASE per project convention — the main driver of the 0.67 convention score. Note: several static-analysis violations attributed to app.py, test_app.py, and repositories.py are pre-existing module-level Flask instances, not introduced here.

Notification enqueue is inlined in the edit_task handler after the update; if the broker is unreachable, send_notification_email.delay() raises and can turn an already-succeeded DB update into a 500, coupling the write path to broker availability. Routing to a dedicated queue mitigates but does not decouple this.
Task parameter is named user_email but callers pass g.current_user.username, so the first argument is semantically ambiguous if username differs from email address.
delay() is patched in every test, so the actual task body is never executed; coverage validates orchestration only, not the task itself.

strengths: Transition-to-completed detection is correct: existing_task is fetched pre-update, and the guard ensures the notification fires exactly once, with a regression test covering repeated completion of an already-completed task.
Pre-fetch plus a 404 guard for missing tasks tightens the existing edit path that previously relied solely on update_task returning None.
Clean module split — celery_config.py for broker settings, notification_tasks.py for the task — with the notification routed to a dedicated 'notifications' queue.
Tests reuse existing register/token_for/auth fixtures and mock delay, keeping the suite fast and hermetic.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, well-tested async-notification integration that respects existing handler/repository/test patterns but introduces minor convention debt (lowercase module constants) and couples the HTTP write path to broker availability via an inlined enqueue; I agree with the measured 0.67 convention score.

problems.description: Half-finished refactor: route handlers now call user_repository/task_repository directly (register, login, auth_required, list_tasks, add_task, show_task, edit_task), but the old delegating wrappers (create_user, find_user, find_user_by_id, create_task, get_tasks, get_task, update_task) still exist in app.py (only fetch_task appears to still route through them), creating two parallel access paths and near-dead code.

Cognitive complexity increased by +15 (SonarQube) despite this being a refactor; the generic BaseRepository + lambda store-accessor indirection added abstraction layers and nesting without reducing the underlying logic, which is counterproductive for a pure-refactor commit.

Repositories are coupled to app.py's module-global _store via lambda accessors (UserRepository(lambda: _store, _store_lock)) and a shared Lock; the extraction partitions CRUD code but does not introduce a storage seam, so the abstraction is partial.

New repositories.py is flagged for 'Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' (the repository instances), and the commit leaves pre-existing convention violations in celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, and test_app.py untouched (convention score holds at 0.67).

strengths: User/Task dataclasses and CRUD logic cleanly extracted into repositories.py, cutting app.py by 87 net lines and adding a clear domain layer.
Unused generate_password_hash import removed from app.py — no dead imports left behind.
Route handlers were consistently migrated to repository calls while preserving the full error-handling flow (400/401/404/409 status paths).
Per SonarQube: no new bugs, no new smells, no duplications; the diff is purely additive (+1 file, +9 imports) with no functional behavior change.
commit_reviews.summary: A directionally sound repository extraction that slims app.py, but it leaves dead delegating wrappers and pushes cognitive complexity up by +15, so it reads as a better-but-unfinished refactor.

problems.description: Cursor pagination in TaskRepository.paginate does a linear O(n) scan (next() over enumerate) to locate the cursor and materializes the full filtered list before slicing; acceptable for the in-memory store but will not scale to a real backing store.
SonarQube cognitive complexity +20 is concentrated in paginate (generator lookup inside try/except plus a nested conditional expression); extractable into a simpler index lookup helper.

Cursor is a task id resolved by linear re-scan rather than a true keyset cursor, so a task deleted between pages turns the next request into a 400; semantics assume no concurrent mutation of the owner's task set.

flask_limiter in_memory_fallback is per-process, so under multiple workers the limit would not be shared; acceptable for the single-process dev app but worth documenting before deploying multi-worker.
rate_limit_key catches only ValueError from decode_token; any other exception type from a malformed/expired token would propagate unhandled from the limiter key function.

strengths: Rate limiting keyed by authenticated user id with IP fallback is a sensible security default that also protects unauthenticated auth endpoints.
Pagination logic lives in the repository layer and reuses existing filtering/sorting via the extracted _ordered_tasks helper, matching the codebase's repository pattern.
Strict input validation (limit 1-100, positive cursor) with clean 400 responses, covered by parametrized tests.
Comprehensive tests: page boundaries, default and max limits, invalid-parameter rejection, and limiter.reset() in the fixture for rate-limit test isolation.
Thread-safe: paginate holds the repository lock while reading, consistent with get_all.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-tested cross-cutting additions (rate limiting + cursor pagination) that respect existing repository/route patterns, though the measured 0.67 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py) rather than anything this commit introduces.

compounding_issues: The Session 2 ownership migration left a permanent 'legacy' compatibility user (random password hash) with NULL-owner tasks reassigned to it; this synthetic-user workaround persists through all later sessions and adds subtle conceptual debt.

Session 2 embedded schema-migration/ownership logic inside init_db() in a single-file layout that Session 4 had to lift out wholesale into UserRepository.initialize_database, forcing a partial rewrite instead of reuse of the migration code.

Default JWT secret ('development-secret-change-me') and Redis rate-limit URL (localhost:6379) remain hardcoded as fallbacks in the final state; acceptable for a demo, but a production footgun if deployed unconfigured.

get_tasks() (created_at DESC ordering) remains defined after Session 5 but is no longer used by the route, which now uses cursor pagination (id DESC ordering) — minor dead code and an ordering inconsistency between the two accessors.
key_decisions: Session 2 established a multi-user ownership model (users table, owner_id, JWT auth with register/login and task isolation), which anchors every subsequent session.
Session 3 integrated asynchronous completion notifications via Celery with a clean seam — tests monkeypatch send_notification_email.delay(), keeping the test suite free of a broker dependency.
Session 4 extracted all SQLite CRUD into a repositories.py layer (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository), the clearest structural improvement and the foundation Session 5 extended.
Session 5 layered cross-cutting production concerns — Redis-backed Flask-Limiter rate limiting (with in-memory fallback) and cursor-based pagination with a total count — plus a JSON 429 handler.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and measurably across the five sessions. Session 1 was a modest hygiene pass over the seed (timezone-aware timestamps, stricter input validation, init_db() on import). Session 2 was the pivotal feature leap — JWT auth and per-user task ownership with careful migration of pre-existing rows to a legacy user. Session 3 added asynchronous completion notifications with correct pending-to-completed transition detection. Session 4 was a clean refactor that shrank app.py from roughly 260 to 160 lines by extracting a repository layer. Session 5 finished strongest, adding rate limiting, cursor pagination, and edge-case validation, and it even fixed its own initially flaky rate-limit test by resetting the limiter between tests. Test coverage grew from 0 to 9 passing tests spanning lifecycle, validation, auth isolation, pagination, and rate limiting. The arc reads as greenfield foundation, then a structural hard pivot to multi-tenancy, then steady consolidation and hardening.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session arc that pivots from a single-user Flask API to a hardened multi-tenant service with auth, async notifications, a repository layer, rate limiting, and pagination — all greenfield decisions anchored the story and later refactors paid off.
